intro: The Light Deck is where every number on the ship starts: how bright is a star, how far away, how hot, and what colour. Every Refregier exam opens with magnitudes and blackbody radiation, so these doors must be fast and automatic. Constants come from the exam table: use SI.

encounters.title: Scales of the sky: AU, parsec, parallax

source.where: Choudhuri §1.1 (mass, length and time scales), §1.3 (coordinates, parallax)

blocks.html: Astronomy measures almost nothing directly except angles and fluxes. Distances, sizes, masses and luminosities are all inferred. The first skill is to move between angles and lengths with the small-angle approximation $\theta\simeq D/d$ (radians).

blocks.label: The parsec is the distance at which 1 AU subtends 1 arcsecond.
Parallax: p is half the yearly back-and-forth shift of a nearby star against the distant background.

blocks.html: Ladder of sizes to keep in your head: Sun $7\times10^8$ m; Earth–Sun 1 AU; nearest star (Proxima) 1.3 pc; Sun–Galactic centre 8 kpc; Milky Way disk radius ~15 kpc; Andromeda 0.77 Mpc; a rich cluster ~2 Mpc across; observable Universe ~$10^4$ Mpc. Each step is roughly a factor of $10^3$–$10^5$.

Angles you will need: $1^\circ=\pi/180$ rad, $1'=1^\circ/60$, $1''=1'/60=4.85\times10^{-6}$ rad. A telescope of diameter $D$ resolves at best $\theta\simeq1.22\lambda/D$ (Rayleigh criterion, diffraction limit); the eye resolves about $1'$.

Parallax halves when distance doubles: $p\propto1/d$ (HS24 summer MC1: four times further means $p/4$, not $p/16$). And for "how far away is a star at $l=180^\circ$" draw the picture: longitude $180^\circ$ points away from the Galactic centre, so distances add.
MC: parallax to distance, Galactic geometry. Open: "how far away would the Sun no longer be resolved" (HS25 winter Q1), "is the Moon resolved by a 6 m CMB telescope at 150 GHz" (HS25 practice Q1).

blocks.html: The eye responds roughly logarithmically, so Hipparchus' brightness classes became a logarithmic scale. Five magnitudes are exactly a factor 100 in flux; a larger magnitude means fainter.

blocks.label: Apparent magnitude compares fluxes. 1 mag = factor 2.512.

blocks.html: The absolute magnitude $M$ is the apparent magnitude the object would have at 10 pc. Since $F\propto L/d^2$, comparing the same object at $d$ and at 10 pc gives the distance modulus. Interstellar dust adds an extinction $A_\lambda>0$ (in magnitudes).

A colour index is a difference of magnitudes in two filters, e.g. $B-V=m_B-m_V$. Small (or negative) $B-V$ means relatively more flux in the bluer $B$ band, i.e. a hotter star. The colour does not depend on distance (both bands dim equally), so it measures temperature, not brightness.

Memorise anchors: $\Delta m=5\Rightarrow100\times$, $\Delta m=2.5\Rightarrow10\times$, $\Delta m=1\Rightarrow2.5\times$, $\Delta m=4\Rightarrow40\times$. The Sun is $m=-26.8$, the faintest naked-eye stars $m\approx6$–$7$. The Sun's absolute magnitude is $M\approx4.8$: a very ordinary star.

Two traps: (1) the sign: brighter = smaller $m$; (2) flux goes as $d^{-2}$, so distance enters with $5\log_{10}$, not $2.5\log_{10}$. Extinction makes $m$ larger (fainter): $m=M+5\log_{10}(d/10\,\mathrm{pc})+A$.
Every exam: flux ratio from $\Delta m$ (MC), distance from $m$ and $M$ (MC), SN Ia apparent magnitude (HS24 summer Q1), limiting distance for the naked eye (HS25 winter Q1b).

check.q: Star S1 has $B-V=0.5$, star S2 has $B-V=1.0$. Which must be true?
options: S1 emits relatively more short-wavelength light than S2
S2 emits relatively more short-wavelength light
check.explain: Smaller $B-V$: relatively brighter in $B$ (blue). Colour says nothing about distance or total brightness.

blocks.html: A blackbody is matter in thermal equilibrium with its radiation: it absorbs everything and emits a spectrum fixed by $T$ alone. Its specific intensity is the Planck function (Choudhuri (2.6)).
Three limits/integrals you must be able to state and use:

blocks.label: Wien displacement, energy density, emergent flux, luminosity. The last one defines the effective temperature of a star.

blocks.html: Increase $T$ and the whole curve moves up and to the right: $\partial B_\nu/\partial T>0$ at every $\nu$ (HS25 winter Q2a), so blackbody curves of different temperature never cross. Hotter stars are brighter at every wavelength and bluer. The RJ tail is linear in $T$: that is why radio astronomers quote brightness as a temperature.

Plot $\log B_
u$ against $\log
u$: a rising straight line of slope 2 (RJ), a peak at $h
u\approx2.8k_BT$, then an exponential cliff (Wien). The CMB (2.73 K) peaks near 160 GHz (mm waves), the Sun (5770 K) near 500 nm in $\lambda$.

$\lambda_{\max}$ from $B_\lambda$ and $ u_{\max}$ from $B_ u$ are not related by $\lambda=c/ u$: the two distributions have different peaks because $d u eq d\lambda$. Use $\lambda_{\max}T=2.898$ mm K only for wavelength peaks. And RJ requires $ u\ll k_BT/h$ (57 GHz for the CMB), so at 100 GHz you must use the full Planck formula.

MC: $u\propto T^4$, colour vs temperature. Open: derive RJ by expanding $e^x\approx1+x$ (HS24 summer Q2a), CMB power on a bolometer, temperature fluctuation from $\partial B/\partial T$, dust vs CMB (HS25 winter Q2), Wien peak of a 10 $M_\odot$ star (Q3).

encounters.title: Why specific intensity is conserved in empty space

source.where: HS25 practice: MC 2 (solution) and Choudhuri §2.2.2 eq. (2.10)

encounters.goal: Show that $I_\nu$ is the same at both ends of a ray in vacuum, and explain why a distant resolved galaxy has the same surface brightness as a nearby one.

steps.prompt: Take two small areas $dA_1$, $dA_2$ perpendicular to the ray, a distance $R$ apart. Write the energy through both, seen from each end.
Express the solid angles through the areas.
Interpret.
steps.reveal: Flux falls as $R^{-2}$ but so does the solid angle of the source; their ratio (surface brightness) is constant. Unresolved stars still look dimmer because their image size is set by diffraction/seeing, not by their true angular size.

keyPoints: flux and solid angle both $\propto R^{-2}$

encounters.title: How far can you still see the Sun?
encounters.problem: The Sun has radius $R_\odot=6.957\times10^8$ m and apparent magnitude $m_\odot=-26.8$ at $1$ AU ($=1.495\times10^{11}$ m). The naked eye resolves $1$ arcmin and detects sources down to $m\sim7$. Ignore extinction and expansion.

steps.prompt: Angular resolution of the eye in radians, $1' = \frac{1}{60}\frac{\pi}{180}$.
steps.hint: $1^\circ=\pi/180$ rad and $1^\circ=60'$. The result is about $2.9\times10^{-4}$.

steps.prompt: Distance at which the Sun (diameter $2R_\odot$) shrinks to $1'$: $\theta\simeq 2R_\odot/d$. Give it in AU.
steps.hint: Small-angle approximation $\theta\simeq D/d$ with $D=2R_\odot$. Then divide by $1\,\text{AU}$.

steps.prompt: Distance at which the Sun fades to $m=7$. From $m_\odot-m = 2.5\log_{10}(F/F_\odot)=5\log_{10}(1\,\text{AU}/d)$. Give it in parsec.
steps.hint: Flux $\propto d^{-2}$, so $\Delta m = 5\log_{10}(d/1\,\text{AU})$. Solve for $d$: $d=1\,\text{AU}\cdot10^{(7-m_\odot)/5}$, then divide by $3.0857\times10^{16}$ m/pc.

encounters.title: A 10 solar-mass star: colour and temperature
encounters.problem: On the main sequence $L\propto M^3$ and $L\propto T_{\rm eff}^6$ (Refregier's scalings). A star has $M=10\,M_\odot$. Take $T_{\rm eff,\odot}=5770$ K and Wien's law $\lambda_{\max}T=b=2.898\times10^{-3}$ m K.

steps.prompt: Surface temperature of the star: eliminate $L$, $T_{\rm eff}\propto M^{1/2}$.
Peak wavelength of the star in nm.
steps.hint: Wien: $\lambda_{\max}=b/T$; multiply by $10^9$ for nm. Sun: 502 nm.

steps.prompt: Ratio $\lambda_{\max,\star}/\lambda_{\max,\odot}$. (Below 1 means the star looks bluer.)

encounters.title: A supernova in Andromeda
encounters.problem: A Type Ia supernova (peak absolute magnitude $M=-19.3$) explodes in Andromeda at $d=765$ kpc. Ignore extinction. Proxima Centauri has $m=11$.

steps.prompt: Apparent magnitude from the distance modulus $m-M=5\log_{10}(d/10\,\text{pc})$.
Flux ratio $F_{\rm SN}/F_{\rm Proxima}$ with $\Delta m = 2.5\log_{10}(F_1/F_2)$.
steps.hint: Fainter objects have the bigger magnitude: $F_{\rm SN}/F_{\rm P}=10^{0.4(m_P-m_{SN})}$. Expect a few hundred.

encounters.title: Is the Moon a good calibrator for a CMB telescope?
encounters.problem: A CMB telescope with a mirror of diameter $D=6$ m observes at $150$ GHz. The Moon spans $0.5^\circ$. Use the Rayleigh criterion $\theta\simeq1.22\lambda/D$.

steps.prompt: Observing wavelength in mm.
Resolution in arcmin.
steps.hint: $\theta=1.22\lambda/D$ in rad, times $180/\pi$ for degrees, times 60 for arcmin.

steps.prompt: How many resolution elements fit across the Moon? ($30'/\theta$)
steps.hint: About 21: the Moon is well resolved, so it is not a point-source calibrator.

encounters.problem: The naked eye sees stars with $m<6.5$. A star with absolute magnitude $M=4$ (a bit brighter than the Sun) is visible out to which distance? No extinction. Within 25 %.

steps.prompt: Limiting distance in pc.

encounters.title: The Sun as a blackbody
encounters.problem: Treat the Sun as a blackbody with $R_\odot=6.957\times10^8$ m and $T_{\rm eff}=5772$ K. $\sigma_{SB}=5.670\times10^{-8}$ W m$^{-2}$ K$^{-4}$.

steps.prompt: Luminosity $L=4\pi R^2\sigma_{SB}T^4$ in units of $10^{26}$ W.
steps.hint: $\approx3.83\times10^{26}$ W: this is how $L_\odot$ is defined in practice.

steps.prompt: Solar constant: flux at 1 AU, in W/m$^2$.

encounters.title: Boss: CMB versus thermal dust (exam problem)

source.where: Open Question 2 [CMB and thermal dust, 10 pt], HS25 winter session

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the final answers. Parts (a) and (c) are graded by you against the key points.
statement: In cosmological observations of fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), thermal dust emission in our galaxy can act as a systematic foreground.

(a) [4 pt] The specific intensity $I_
u$ of thermal emission of an optically thick object depends only on its temperature $T$ and is given by $B_
u(T)= rac{2h}{c^2} rac{
u^3}{e^{h
u/k_BT}-1}$. Show that for all frequencies $
u$ this specific intensity increases as the temperature increases.

(b) [4 pt] The CMB is observed as a near perfect blackbody of temperature $T_{\rm CMB}=2.73$ K. A typical CMB intensity fluctuation has amplitude $10^{-5}B_\nu(T_{\rm CMB})$. Dust in our galaxy is observed at $T_d=20$ K. Assuming this dust emission is also optically thick everywhere, show that at $\nu=100$ GHz the dust emission would be $\sim1.8\times10^6$ times brighter than the CMB fluctuation.

(c) [2 pt] The dust is not optically thick but a modified blackbody (greybody): $I_
u=	au_
u B_
u(T_d)$ with $	au_
u=	au_{353}(
u/353\,	ext{GHz})^ eta$. With $T_d=20$ K and $ eta=1.6$, for what values of $	au_{353}$ would the CMB fluctuation be brighter than the dust at $
u=100$ GHz?
